title: The Taizé chants
hook: short, repeated chants from an ecumenical community of brothers in a French village

segments.voice: Yesterday, Quaker silence, and George Fox's line, that of God in every one. Did you find one thing worth answering in someone hard? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

Ubi caritas et amor. A long, low church, almost dark, with candles on the floor up front and people sitting on the ground, a lot of them young, backpacks against the wall. A line is sung. It ends. It starts again. Same words, same tune. And again. Nobody seems to be in a hurry for verse two, because there isn't one. After a while, people stop reading the words off the sheet. A while longer, and some have their eyes closed. This is evening prayer in Taizé, a small village in France. Yesterday the sound of prayer was silence. Today it's a single line, sung until it stops being something you read and becomes something you know.
screen: `A LOW CHURCH, CANDLES ON THE FLOOR.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `THE SHEET GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: Taizé is home to a community of brothers, men who live together under vows, founded by a Swiss Protestant known as Brother Roger. From the start it was meant to be ecumenical, a place where Christians from different churches could pray together. Today the brothers come from Protestant and Catholic backgrounds, and young people come to spend a week living and praying with them. Here are the chants, four ways. First, they're short. A Taizé chant is often a single line, sometimes just a few words, some taken straight from scripture or from old prayers. Second, they repeat. A chant is sung over and over, sometimes for several minutes. The repetition is the point. Once nobody has to think about the next verse, attention can go somewhere else. Third, the languages. The chants are sung in many languages, including Latin. Some are very old words in new music. Ubi caritas, for example, is an old Latin hymn text: "Ubi caritas et amor, Deus ibi est," where charity and love are, God is there. Others echo the Psalms, like Psalm 117: "O praise the LORD, all ye nations: praise him, all ye people." Fourth, the silence in the middle. A Taizé prayer usually has a Bible reading and then a long silence, set among the chants. The singing leads into the quiet and back out of it. The brothers have said they hope a chant keeps going after the prayer ends, hummed under the breath while working or walking. That's how a short line becomes a companion for the day.
screen: `SHORT: OFTEN A SINGLE LINE.` · `REPEATED UNTIL IT SINKS IN.` · `MANY LANGUAGES, OLD WORDS.` · `A SILENCE IN THE MIDDLE.` · then, large: `UBI CARITAS ET AMOR, DEUS IBI EST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hum one short chant. Choose one line. If you pray, Ubi caritas works, or any short line you already know from your own tradition. If not, a single line of any song that steadies you. Hum it or sing it softly, then let it end, and start it again, same tune, same words. Don't add verses. Don't perform. Let your breath shape the line. By the third or fourth time, notice whether you're still reading it in your head, or just singing it. The bell holds the time.
The Taizé chants. Short lines, often from scripture or old prayers, sung over and over at the ecumenical community in Taizé, with silence in the middle. Today's word.
Your line: sing it again. Today, keep your one short line going under your breath while you wash a dish or walk to the car. When it fades, sing it again. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: At Taizé and in Taizé-style services elsewhere, people sing short chants many times over, hear a short Bible reading, and keep a long silence together, often by candlelight.

notes: Only the medieval Latin text of Ubi caritas and KJV Psalm 117:1 are quoted. Taizé's own musical settings and any modern lyrics are under copyright and are not quoted; the practice invites humming a short line, not reproducing Taizé music.
